title.value: Iwaru on the tide count and on nine years of quiet in a grade

description.value: Interview with the keeper of the tide count at the Lower Midden on how a grade goes quiet after a wall fails. Iwaru describes moving the count so that a failure fell in another grade's section.

content.value:
Q. Could you say that again more quietly, for the recorder?

A. No. Said quietly it is not the same thing said softly, it is not a thing. If you want it small, stand further off.

Q. Then tell us what happened three days inland.

A. There is no inland here past a day, in the mouth or on the ground. Ask me about water and about who was standing where and you will get everything I have.

Q. The eleventh section. Who was standing where?

A. The wall went at the third low water of the season. It took the garden below it and it took two people who were on the wrong side of it, and the grade has not spoken about it in nine years.

Q. What does it mean for a grade to be quiet?

A. That nobody says the thing and everybody works as if it had been said. It is not a silence. It is a full room.

Q. You keep the count. Where does the failure sit in it?

A. Four tides earlier than it happened.

Q. Why?

A. Because four tides earlier the section was in the previous grade's holding, and the previous grade is dead and cannot lose anything further. The grade that is alive has children in it.

Q. Does anyone else know the count was moved?

A. The count is kept by one person so that this question has one answer. You have it.

consentNote.value: Iwaru consented to the recording of the whole exchange, including the last four answers, and asked only that the survey not repeat any of it within earshot of the walls, which at conversational range on drained ground is a larger area than it sounds.
